newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sergeant's rape case seen going to jury Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sergeant's rape case seen going to jury Wednesday.

text.p: Defence attorneys and prosecutors in the rape trial of Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson wrangled Wednesday over instructions to the military jury, which was expected to begin deliberations later in the day.

The six-member jury, which will be asked to rule on 19 charges of rape and 35 other counts against Simpson, will get the case following closing arguments and instructions Wednesday afternoon, defence attorney Maj. Mike Sawyers said.
"They'll begin (deliberations) tonight, I'm almost positive," Sawyers said after a morning court session.

Simpson, 32, is the first of 12 trainers charged in a sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground to go to trial, although four other cases have been resolved through administrative means or plea agreements. He also faces the most rape charges, involving six women.
He has pleaded innocent to rape and the other charges, but earlier pleaded guilty to 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five counts of propositioning.

Testimony in the case ended Tuesday, after eight days in which prosecutors sought to show Simpson abused his authority to force female trainees at the proving ground's Ordnance Centre and School into having sex with him.
His lawyers argued that Simpson engaged only in consensual sex with the women.
Wednesday's morning court session was devoted to hammering out fine points of the instructions given to the jury and the findings they will be permitted to reach.

Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston said he would allow jurors to consider, in instances where Simpson has been charged with rape, verdicts on lesser charges of indecent assault. He rejected a prosecution request to allow jurors also to consider a verdict on indecent assault.

An Army legal liaison told reporters after the session that Johnston would not in his instructions broaden the military rape law to remove a requirement that a fear of death or bodily harm must be present to justify a lack of resistance by the woman involved.

Johnston last week said a drill sergeant's power over trainees created a "unique situation" and rejected a defence request to dismiss rape charges involving four women who had not explicitly resisted sex with Simpson. This sparked speculation he would create a broader definition of rape.

Simpson faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted of rape. He faces a total maximum sentence of 32 years, dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the counts to which he has pleaded guilty.

Although the National Organisation for the Advancement of Coloured People and other civil rights supporters have said the investigation that led to charges against Simpson, who is African-American, and the other trainers unfairly targeted blacks in the military, race has not been presented as an issue in the trial.
